summary: Robert Moran profiles Eli Roth's slasher film Thanksgiving, which grew out of a fake trailer in the 2007 double-feature Grindhouse and is finally made after years of fan demand. Roth explains how Black Friday "trample videos" inspired a 13-minute opening that critiques consumerism and nods to Dawn of the Dead. The piece also covers Roth's career, his love of slashers and his acting-informed approach to directing.
one_line: Eli Roth turns his Grindhouse fake trailer into the slasher Thanksgiving, opening with a Black Friday sale massacre that satirises consumerism and evokes Dawn of the Dead.
key_facts: Eli Roth first introduced Thanksgiving (tagline: "There will be no leftovers") 16 years ago as a spoof trailer in the middle of Grindhouse, Quentin Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez's 2007 double-feature.
Roth and co-writer Jeff Rendell grew up in Massachusetts, where Thanksgiving is a huge deal with pilgrim recreation villages, school plays and parades.
The film's killer wears a mask of John Carver, the first governor of the first US settlement and a real governor on the Mayflower, and wields an axe in modern-day Plymouth, Massachusetts.
Roth says fans badgering him year after year is why Thanksgiving became a real movie; the trailer was called "the best horror movie never made".
The film's key creative breakthrough came from online Black Friday "trample videos" that began proliferating on social media around a decade ago.
The film opens with 13 minutes set amid a Black Friday sale, which the reviewer calls possibly the most horribly enjoyable 13 minutes of a film all year.
The rampaging mall shoppers nod to George Romero's Dawn of the Dead (1978), and the scenes also evoke images from the US's January 6 riots.
Roth argues Black Friday desperation stems from the lack of a middle class, with the few at the top watching "all the rats fighting over these crumbs".
Roth grew up on Freddie, Jason, Michael Myers and Chucky, and wanted "a new killer in town"; he names Mute Witness (1995) as one of his favourites.
Roth's film Hostel (2005) spawned the term "torture porn"; his feature debut was Cabin Fever (2002).
The reviewer recalls attending a Cabin Fever Q&A at Glebe's now defunct Valhalla cinema about 20 years ago; Roth remembers meeting Leigh Whannell, who said he'd made a short film called Saw.
Roth has directed over 20 films, produced more than double that, and acted as Sgt. Donny "The Bear Jew" Donowitz in Inglourious Basterds (2009) and a Live Nation rep in The Idol.
Roth finished The Idol right before directing Thanksgiving and says acting makes him an "actor's director" who lets the cast go off-script.
